title: The Confessions, Rousseau
subject: litterature
description: Rousseau recounts his life with unprecedented sincerity. The Confessions invented modern autobiography and opened the way to romanticism.

hero.hook: “I am forming a company that never had an example”: this is how the modern autobiography begins.

blocks.text: The **Confessions** by **Jean-Jacques Rousseau**, published posthumously between **1782** and **1789**, mark the birth of modern autobiography. Rousseau recounts his own life. The “me” becomes an object of literary investigation, not just a pretext to talk about History.

Rousseau breaks with aristocratic memoirs, stories of great people glorifying their actions, and religious confessions, confessions made to God. He seeks self-understanding, not just forgiveness. The book covers his childhood in Geneva, his years of wandering and his career as a philosophical writer.

“I form a company that never had an example”: Rousseau defines the , the author's commitment to telling the truth about himself, later theorized by Philippe Lejeune. He tells his life for its own sake, not to glorify History through him. **[[autobiographical pact]]**

blocks.caption: Jean-Jacques Rousseau: radical sincerity and solitude.

blocks.text: Obsessed with the security of his manuscript, Rousseau often traveled with the pages of the Confessions clutched to him in a canvas bag.

Unlike the **Confessions of Saint Augustine**, Christian model of confession in the 4th century, the judge is no longer God but the reader. Rousseau secularizes confession and invents authenticity as a supreme value. Truth lies in faithfulness to feelings, not just objective facts.

Rousseau confesses to the theft of a ribbon, his taste for flogging at **Miss Lambercier**, his relationship with , a woman who welcomed him at 16 and became his protector, whom he calls “Mom”. He also admits to the abandonment of his five children to the **Foundlings**, a Parisian hospice. **[[Mme de Warens]]**

blocks.caption: Nature in Rousseau: mirror of a solitary soul.

blocks.text: By saying all the bad things about himself, he takes away from his enemies the power to denounce him. The landscape becomes the mirror of a new sensitivity, the basis of , a movement which exalts feelings and nature, and of nostalgia for lost time. **[[Romanticism]]**

Rousseau wrote the second part in exile, his books burned in Paris and Geneva. Convinced of a universal conspiracy against him, he seeks to rehabilitate his memory in the face of his detractors, including **Voltaire**.

He presents himself as the man from : naturally good, perverted by a hypocritical society. Rousseau believed that man is good by nature and that it is society that corrupts him. The reader becomes complicit in a passionate defense. Voltaire, in an anonymous pamphlet, revealed the abandonment of his children, forcing Rousseau to publicly confess and accept his contradictions. **[[Rousseauism and the "noble savage"]]**

The influence is immense: **Chateaubriand**, **Stendhal**, **George Sand**, **Goethe**, **Tolstoy**. Rousseau prefigures **Freud**, founder of psychoanalysis, by showing that childhood and sexuality shape the character of the adult.
It sanctifies the individual: every life, even modest, deserves to be told. This democratization of the subject nourishes the diary and, later, contemporary self-exposure on social networks.

By daring to say “I” without a heroic mask, Rousseau opens the way to diaries and first-person novels. Confession becomes a genre in its own right, and personal truth a literary value. Even his contradictions, defender of childhood but absent father, are part of the project: showing a real man, not a model.
The **Confessions** invent modern autobiography by placing psychological sincerity and childhood at the heart of literature, in the face of a society deemed corrupting.
